raw_response:
I've been farming these 10 mu for 20 years now, ever since I married into this village at 25. My husband and my oldest son work construction over in the county town, so most days it's me and my mother-in-law — she's 72 but still strong — doing the field work. We have seven people under this roof, including two grandchildren, so we can't afford to mess around. Every yuan I spend on the field is a yuan I don't have for medicine or school fees.

I don't read or write, but I know this land. I know which spots stay wet and which dry out first. I know that old Zhang down the lane always gets his wheat in a few days before me and his yields are usually good, so I watch what he does. Last year my wheat did about 400 jin per mu — not great, not terrible. The maize did a bit better, maybe 450 jin. I keep some of our own wheat seed, but for maize I always buy new hybrid seed from the shop. You can't save maize seed, everyone knows that.

**Wheat:** I'll plant the whole 10 mu to wheat, same as always. I don't have the cash or the nerve to try cotton or vegetables — one bad year and we'd be in real trouble. I aim to get it in around the 10th of October, before the cold comes. I hire Old Li's tractor to plow after the maize comes off, then I broadcast the seed by hand — about 40 jin per mu, seed I bought from the village supply store. It costs me, but the saved seed wasn't looking good this year.

For fertilizer, I do what I've always done: before planting I spread one big bag of that compound fertilizer for every two mu — that's about 20 kg per mu. Then when the wheat turns green in March, if it looks a bit yellow I spread another bag of urea for every two mu, about 20 kg per mu. I know some people put on more, but fertilizer is expensive and my son's wages don't always come regular. I'd rather put on a little less and make sure we have cash if someone gets sick.

Water: I'll irrigate three times if I can afford the electricity — once when the wheat wakes up in spring, once at jointing when the heads are forming, and once when the grain is filling. The well is good here, but the pump meter runs fast and my brother-in-law says the price keeps going up. If money is tight in May, I might skip that last irrigation and hope for rain.

For weeds, I spray herbicide once in early spring. If I see aphids later, I'll buy some insecticide, but I watch first — sometimes it's not bad enough to spend the money.

**Maize:** The wheat comes off around June 10th, and I have to get the maize in quick — sometimes the same day, usually within two or three days. There's no time for deep plowing. Old Li runs the rotary tiller shallow over the stubble, and we plant right away. I buy hybrid seed from the shop — one small bag per mu, about 2 to 3 jin. 

For maize fertilizer, I put compound fertilizer in the row at planting — about 15 kg per mu, a bit less than the wheat gets. Then when the corn is knee-high, about a month later, I side-dress urea, another 15 kg per mu. Some years if the rain is good I might skip the top-dress, but last year I didn't top-dress and the yield was disappointing, so this year I'll do it.

Irrigation for maize — I'll plan for two times. July is the rainy season, so sometimes nature does the work. But if it's dry at tasseling, I pump water. If it's a wet summer, maybe I only irrigate once. I spray herbicide right after planting, and I watch for corn borer. If the leaves start looking shredded, I buy spray.

Labor is mostly me and my mother-in-law. At harvest, though, I hire three or four people for a few days because my husband can't always get leave from the construction site. Hired labor is 120 yuan a day now — it adds up fast.

My biggest worry is always cash at planting time. I have to buy seed and fertilizer in October and June when money is tight. If the wheat price stays low this year, next spring I'll be squeezing every coin. But this is our life. We do what we did last year, we watch our neighbors, and we pray the weather holds.
